stories.headline: Spoofed vessel identity appeared near the entrance channel at Port Aransas two weeks before jetty blast
stories.dek: Public AIS data places the borrowed fishing-vessel identity close to the entrance channel in mid-October. The Coast Guard declined to comment on any connection to the Oct. 28 explosion.
body: Public AIS records reviewed by maritime analysts show that the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel at Port Aransas overnight Oct. 14-15, about two weeks before an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel.

Gulfwater reported the anomaly Oct. 22. On the same night the identity was logged off Port Aransas, the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Independent analyst Ian McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander, said then that the pattern was consistent with identity spoofing. A closer review of the public track places the signal near the entrance channel.

"The data tells you where a signal was. It does not tell you who sent it or why," McCready said Monday. "Two weeks is a long gap, and I would be careful drawing a straight line. But the location is close to the entrance, and that is worth writing down."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the explosion. "We are not going to discuss matters under investigation," Ruiz said. "Our focus is the safety of the waterway."

The Navy said Saturday that the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams and the Coast Guard are working the channel jointly; the FBI is investigating.

Port status as of Monday morning: the channel remains closed at the entrance, with no reopening date announced. Crude loadings at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, have been halted since the closure. Inbound traffic is holding offshore.

AIS is a cooperative system. A transponder broadcasts whatever identity it is programmed with, and shore and satellite receivers record it. Analysts detect spoofing by finding the same identity in two places at once, as in this case. Gulfwater has not identified the vessel that transmitted the Pelican Ridge identity and makes no assessment of who was aboard.

stories.headline: Analysts flag ship-signal anomaly near Texas port weeks before blast; officials decline comment
stories.dek: A fishing vessel's identity was broadcast near the Corpus Christi entrance channel two weeks before an explosive device damaged a tug there. Federal officials would not discuss any connection.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Maritime analysts said Monday that a fishing vessel's electronic identity was broadcast near the entrance to one of the nation's busiest energy ports about two weeks before an explosion there closed the channel, but federal officials declined to say whether the two are connected.

The blast happened around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. On Saturday the Navy attributed the explosion to an explosive device, and its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have since been sweeping the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

Public ship-tracking data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas in mid-October while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts have described the pattern as consistent with identity spoofing. On Monday they noted the signal appeared near the entrance channel.

"It's a data point, not a conclusion," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Public tracking can show you a mismatch. It can't show you intent."
The Coast Guard declined to comment on any link. The FBI would say only that it is investigating, according to Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for its Houston Division.

The closure has stopped crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It has also delayed, for a second time, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation. The brigade's movement was first postponed on Sept. 11, three days before Hurricane Rafael's landfall.
Officials have not said who placed the device or why, and the FBI declined further comment.

stories.headline: Port Aransas waits it out as Navy teams search the channel
stories.dek: Four days after the blast at the jetties, the island is quiet. A bait shop owner who heard it says the waiting is the hard part.
body: The jetties are quiet Monday. No tankers. No tugs. Just gulls, a stiff north wind and a few people standing on the beach road watching Navy and Coast Guard boats work the channel.

Bill Hargrove has watched that water for most of his 64 years. His shop, Hargrove Bait & Tackle, sits a short walk from the jetties. Rafael gutted it in September, and he is still selling hooks and ice from a folding table while he rebuilds.

He was asleep at home when the blast came around 1 a.m. Thursday. "It wasn't thunder. I know thunder," Hargrove says. "It was one big thump, and then every dog on the island started in. I laid there thinking, well, that's not a storm, so what is it?"

The Navy says the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay was caused by an explosive device. Two crew members were hurt. Navy teams trained in explosives and mine clearance are working the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

For the island, the closure lands on top of a storm that already took the fall season. "First the water came in the shop. Then the oil. Now nobody can go in or out of the pass," Hargrove says. "I keep telling people we're open. Open for what, they ask me. Fair question."
He says customers mostly want to talk. "Everybody's got a theory. I tell them I sell bait, not theories."

What you need to know: The ship channel is closed to all traffic until the Coast Guard says otherwise. No reopening date has been announced. Crude exports from the port remain halted. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, keep your distance and call 911.

stories.headline: Why clearing a ship channel takes time, and what it means for a brigade that is still waiting
stories.dek: Navy teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel after last week's blast. Officials won't put a date on reopening, and a Fort Hood brigade's equipment is waiting on it.
body: From the seawall at Port Aransas, the work looks slow. Small boats move back and forth across the mouth of the channel, stop, and move again. That pace is the point.

Since the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused the Oct. 28 blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating the explosion itself.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, would not describe the methods or equipment in use, citing safety and the ongoing investigation. "Our teams will search every yard of that channel they need to," Moreau said. "We are not going to rush it, and we are not going to put a date on it. When we say it is clear, we want it to be clear."

Clearing a channel is not the same as finding one object. Teams have to be confident that nothing else is there before the Coast Guard can let deep-draft ships back through. In a channel that carries tankers, cargo ships and military equipment, the cost of being wrong is measured in lives as well as dollars.

That caution has consequences up the road at Fort Hood. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment were supposed to pass through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer on the way to an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael closed in, and delayed again after last week's blast.

"Our soldiers and their equipment are ready to go," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "We'll move when the port is ready, and not before." Price declined to discuss timelines or where the brigade's equipment is staged.

For military families on the Coastal Bend and at Fort Hood, the delay is another stretch of not knowing. For the port, which has served as a strategic military seaport for decades, it is another week with its gate closed and its cranes idle. Officials say the search will set the schedule, not the other way around.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings stay halted as channel search continues
stories.dek: The second export stoppage since Hurricane Rafael has no end date. An analyst says there is no substitute route at the port's scale.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Tuesday as Navy teams continued searching the ship channel after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, with no reopening date announced.

The halt is the port's second since Hurricane Rafael. Exports stopped when the Coast Guard closed the channel ahead of the storm in September and resumed only after a partial reopening in mid-October, when a backlog of vessels was still working through the offshore anchorage.
Analysts estimate the port moves about half of all U.S. crude exports. The Navy said Saturday that the blast beside a harbor tug was caused by an explosive device.

"There isn't a second door at this scale," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Every day the channel stays shut, barrels that would have left Corpus Christi either sit in tanks or wait for a ship that can't get in. You can move some volume elsewhere along the coast, but not all of it, and not quickly."

Holloway said the market's main question had shifted from damage to duration. "After the storm, people were asking what broke. Now they are asking how long a search takes, and nobody will give them a number. That's the right answer for safety. It's a hard answer for a cargo schedule."

Tankers that would normally queue at the offshore anchorage are holding as they wait for the channel to reopen. Buyers with cargoes booked from the port are weighing whether to wait or seek supply elsewhere, Holloway said.
The Coast Guard has not given a timeline. Officials have said the channel will reopen when it is safe.

stories.headline: 'One second it was a normal night': Injured deckhand, tug captain describe blast at the jetties
stories.dek: Eddie Fontenot, 29, is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. His captain, Ray Dupree, says his first thought was his crew.
body: Eddie Fontenot does not remember hitting the deck of the tug Corrin Bay. He remembers the sound.

"One second it was a normal night," said Fontenot, 29, a deckhand for Laguna Towing, speaking by phone Tuesday from a Corpus Christi hospital where he is recovering from a broken arm and a concussion. "Then it was loud, and then I was looking at the sky. That's what I got."

Fontenot was one of two crew members injured when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy announced Saturday that an explosive device was to blame. Since then, Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel alongside the Coast Guard while the FBI investigates. The Coast Guard closed the channel after the blast, and it remains closed.
Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, the tug's master, has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He said the blast came off the port bow.

"The boat lifted, and the water came up over the rail," Dupree said. "You don't think. You count heads. I had everybody accounted for in under a minute, and then I started worrying about the hull." He declined to discuss the condition of the tug, saying that was for the company and investigators.
Dupree said he has been asked many times what caused the explosion. "I drive a tugboat," he said. "The people whose job it is to answer that are out there right now. I'm going to let them do it."
Fontenot kept his answers short. Asked what he wanted people to know, he paused. "That Cap got us home," he said. "And that I'm going back out. Not this week. But I'm going back."
Dupree said he visits Fontenot most days. "He's tough. He's tougher than me," the captain said. "He keeps asking when he can work. I keep telling him when the doctor says so, and not a day before."
Laguna Towing did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

stories.headline: A port on pause: closed channel ripples from crude docks to relief freight
stories.dek: The Port of Corpus Christi says it is ready to work around the clock once the channel reopens. A freight forwarder who waited a month for relief cargo says customers keep asking for a date he can't give.
body: For the second time this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi is open for business with no way for ships to reach it.

The ship channel has been closed at the entrance since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy teams are searching it with the Coast Guard, and no reopening date has been announced. Crude loadings, which account for most of the port's traffic and about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted.

"Our docks, our cranes and our people are ready," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is closed at the entrance, and nothing moves in or out until the Coast Guard says it is safe. The day it opens, we will be working around the clock to clear the line."

The pause reaches beyond oil. Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, a freight forwarder that handled relief containers after Rafael, has been here before. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider sat at the offshore anchorage for weeks after the storm and berthed Oct. 17, about a month late.

"I learned one lesson from the Gulf Provider, and it's that the cargo can be ready and the water can still say no," Akins said. "I've got customers calling every morning for a date. I tell them the truth. I don't have one, and anybody who gives you one is guessing."
Akins said some shippers are asking about trucking cargo in from other ports, which costs more and takes longer. "Everything that comes in by water to this town, somebody is waiting on," he said.
Salinas said the port's cargo customers have been understanding. "Safety sets the schedule," he said. "We would rather open a day late than open wrong."
The FBI is investigating the blast, which the Navy has attributed to an explosive device.

stories.headline: Bays closed by oil, pass closed by a blast: an Aransas Pass shrimper runs out of water
stories.dek: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael. Seven weeks later, the bays are still closed to fishing and the pass to the Gulf is shut too.
body: Every morning, Huy Nguyen walks the deck of his shrimp boat at the Aransas Pass harbor the way his father did. He checks the lines, the engine, the nets. Then he goes home, because there is nowhere to take the boat.
"Bays closed for oil. Pass closed for the bomb," said Nguyen, 51. "Where do I go? You tell me where, I go tomorrow."

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Sept. 18, days after oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal spread across about 33 square miles of water and shoreline in Rafael's surge. The closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, but the closure remains in place.

Hours earlier that day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel at the entrance. The Navy has said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. For boats based at Aransas Pass, that entrance is the way out to the Gulf.
Nguyen started the season with what he called a fair run, squeezed by diesel prices. He keeps a spiral notebook of every trip, catch and fuel bill. The pages since mid-September are mostly blank.
"I write the date and I write 'no trip,'" he said. "My father would think I am lazy. I am not lazy. The water is closed."

He still owes on the boat and on the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two kids. He said he has not looked for other work yet because he does not know how long the closures will last. "If they tell me three months, I find something. If they tell me next week, I wait. Nobody tells me anything."

The bay shrimp season in Texas runs into late fall, so for families like Nguyen's, each week of closure is a week of the year's income gone. Shrimpers in the area say they want two things: a date, and a way to be made whole for the season they lost.
"Oil, I understand. A storm, I understand," Nguyen said. "This other thing, I don't understand. I just want to fish."

stories.headline: This week: depot back at full production, station power steady, brigade still waiting on the channel
stories.dek: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville, one week after the blast at the jetties.
body: It has been a long fall, and this week brought at least one piece of good news: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"Our workforce has been through a hurricane, a damaged hangar and weeks of standing by, and they came back every time," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "Parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi has been a big part of getting the lines moving again. We're grateful to our neighbors there and to the families who carried a lot while we got here."

At NAS Corpus Christi, power has been steady since the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption last month. Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer, said the cause remains under review. "Power was restored, and base services are operating," Hale said. "We'll share what we can when the review is complete."

The channel: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed after the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy has said the blast was caused by an explosive device. The Coast Guard is working with Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams to search the channel. We will not report on their work beyond what public affairs releases, and we ask readers to do the same on social media.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the port for an overseas rotation has been delayed again by the closure. Fort Hood has not announced a new date. Families with loved ones in the brigade should rely on their unit's family readiness channels for updates.

Around the bases: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. Sunday, so set your clocks back an hour. Several readers have asked about a fall community gathering; we will print details when organizers confirm them.
If the past two months have been heavy for your household, you are not alone. Chaplains and family support staff are available on both installations. Reach out early, and check on your neighbors.

stories.headline: Seven weeks after Rafael, ER visits from bayside neighborhoods are still running high
stories.dek: Emergency room traffic has eased across most of Nueces County. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, health officials say visits remain about 40% above normal.
body: Most of Corpus Christi's emergency rooms have settled back into their usual rhythm since Hurricane Rafael. The exception is the neighborhoods that waited longest for help after the storm.

Emergency room visits are back near normal countywide except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they remain about 40% above normal, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said last week. Stomach illness tied to the boil-water weeks began easing in late September, and the citywide boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

"When one part of the county recovers and another part doesn't, that tells us something, even before we know exactly what," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "We're looking at it closely. In the meantime, if you're sick, please don't wait until it becomes an emergency. A clinic visit early is better than an ER visit late."
Residents of those neighborhoods reported waiting days for help after the storm, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, who runs a relief hub from her church fellowship hall near the bay, said she sees the pattern at her door. "People put off the doctor because the doctor is two buses away and they have a shift," she said. "Then it's the ER at midnight. I've driven more people to the emergency room this fall than in the last five years."
Whitfield said many families are still living in damp rentals while they wait on landlords and repairs. "You can't separate the house from the health," she said.

Shah said residents should seek care for symptoms that linger, keep a list of their medications, and call ahead to clinics about same-day appointments. She also urged people cleaning flood-damaged homes to wear gloves and masks and to keep children away from wet drywall and debris.
"The storm was seven weeks ago," Shah said. "For some families, the recovery started a lot later than that."

stories.headline: Navy teams find second explosive device near entrance channel, render it safe
stories.dek: No one was hurt. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel stays closed while the search continues.
body: Navy teams have found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard say Friday.
No one is hurt. The channel remains closed to all traffic.

"Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," says Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. "No one was injured. The search of the channel continues, and it will continue until we are confident it is complete."
Moreau would not describe the device or where exactly it was found, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The find comes eight days after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were hurt in that blast. The Navy has said it was caused by an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says the closure stays in place. "The channel will reopen when the search is complete and the Captain of the Port is satisfied it is safe," Ruiz says. "We are not giving a date today."

What this means for you: The ship channel is still closed. Crude exports from the port are still halted. There is no change to roads, bridges or beach access announced by officials. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, don't touch it. Keep your distance and call 911.
Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more.

stories.headline: Navy finds, disables second explosive device at entrance to major Texas energy port
stories.dek: The discovery near Corpus Christi extends a closure that has halted crude exports and delayed an Army brigade's overseas rotation.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe Friday, officials said, eight days after an explosion beside a harbor tug closed one of the country's most important energy ports.
"No one was injured. The search of the channel continues," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. She declined to describe the device, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The first explosion went off around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay and damaging the vessel. The Navy later said an explosive device was responsible, and the search by its explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, alongside the Coast Guard, has not let up since.
The FBI is investigating, its Houston Division spokesperson, Mark Ellery, confirmed. "We are not going to discuss evidence," he said.

The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and loadings have been halted since the blast. The closure has also delayed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's planned movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation, a movement already postponed once by Hurricane Rafael in September.

Earlier this week, maritime analysts noted that a fishing vessel's identity had been broadcast near the entrance channel about two weeks before the blast, while the vessel itself reported a position hundreds of miles away. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"A second device changes the confidence level, not the timeline, because there isn't one," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Markets were hoping for a date. Today they got a reason it isn't coming yet."
Officials have not said when the channel will reopen.

stories.headline: Second device rendered safe near the Port Aransas jetties; Coast Guard keeps channel closed
stories.dek: Navy teams recovered a second explosive device Friday. Port condition unchanged: entrance closed to all traffic, no reopening date.
body: Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel at Port Aransas Friday and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard said. No injuries were reported. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all traffic.

Port condition as of Friday afternoon: the entrance is closed under Coast Guard order. Inbound and outbound deep-draft movements are suspended. Crude loadings at the port are halted. No reopening date has been issued.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the Captain of the Port would not lift the closure until the full search is complete. "A second find does not shorten the process. It confirms why we follow it," Ruiz said. "When the channel opens, mariners will receive notice through the usual channels."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams continue to work with the Coast Guard. She declined to describe the device or its position, citing safety and the investigation.
The first device detonated around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 alongside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, injuring two of its crew and damaging the tug. The FBI is investigating that blast.

As Gulfwater reported Monday, public AIS data shows the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcast near the entrance channel overnight Oct. 14-15, while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts describe that pattern as consistent with spoofing. Asked Friday whether investigators were examining the AIS observations, Ruiz said the Coast Guard would not comment on any link. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.

Operators with vessels holding offshore should continue to monitor Coast Guard broadcast notices for changes in port condition. After a long closure, a staged restart is typical, with the order of vessel movements set by the Coast Guard and the port.

stories.headline: A second device, a longer wait: what Friday's find means for the Fort Hood brigade
stories.dek: The Navy rendered a second explosive device safe near the channel entrance. A brigade's helicopters and equipment, already delayed twice, wait on the full sweep.
body: When the Navy announced Friday that its teams had found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the news landed in two places at once: on the docks at the port, and about 230 miles north at Fort Hood.

One of the post's aviation brigades had been due to send its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer, bound for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael pushed the movement back in September, and the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties delayed it again.

"We knew the search would take what it takes," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers and families have been patient through a hurricane and now this. The brigade is ready. When the port is ready, we go." He declined to discuss the brigade's schedule, staging or destination beyond describing the mission as an overseas rotation.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, said no one was injured Friday and the search continues. She would not describe the device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been working the channel with the Coast Guard since the Navy said Oct. 30 that the Oct. 28 blast was caused by an explosive device.

Military logisticians plan around tides, cranes and berths. They do not plan around a closed channel with no reopening date. A second find means the Coast Guard is unlikely to reopen until teams are confident they have covered every stretch of water ships will use, and the Navy has said it will not put a date on that.

Locally, the military picture has been improving. Corpus Christi Army Depot returned to full production last week with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. But the depot fixes helicopters; it does not move them overseas. That still depends on the channel.

For families of soldiers in the brigade, the uncertainty is familiar. Price said the Army would announce the movement through public channels once it begins. "Nobody's going to hear it from a rumor first if we can help it," he said.

stories.headline: Port Aransas, gutted by Rafael, loses its fall to a closed channel
stories.dek: A storm took the island's buildings in September. The blast at the jetties and a second device found Friday have taken the boats, the anglers and the fall visitors.
body: PORT ARANSAS — On a normal first Saturday of November, the jetties would be lined with anglers chasing bull redfish, the charter boats would be booked, and the line at the fish-cleaning station would stretch back to the parking lot.

This Saturday, the beach road was mostly quiet. A few people walked dogs. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard boats worked the channel, as they have since an explosion beside a harbor tug around 1 a.m. Oct. 28 closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. On Friday, Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance and rendered it safe. The channel remains closed, with no reopening date.

"In September, the water took the buildings. Now it's taking the customers," said Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties. Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm came ashore on Mustang Island Sept. 14. He has been selling ice, hooks and live bait from a folding table while he rebuilds.

"Summer was good. I'll say that. Summer was real good," Hargrove said. "Then fall showed up with a storm, an oil spill and whatever this is. I've been on this island my whole life. I don't have a word for this year."

Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill. Anglers who might have fished the Gulf side instead are kept off the water near the entrance by the closure. A charter captain who asked not to be named because he was negotiating with his lender said he had refunded every November booking. A waitress at a beach-road cafe said Friday night's crowd was "mostly contractors and reporters."

Hargrove said the second device rattled people more than the first. "The first one, everybody figured it was a one-time thing. A second one, you start looking at the water different," he said. "But I'll tell you what. The boys on those Navy boats, they're the ones out there. I'm just standing on the beach."
Hargrove said he plans to keep the folding table open on weekends. "If somebody wants shrimp and ice, I'm here," he said. "Directions are still free."
Clocks fall back an hour at 2 a.m. Sunday, as daylight saving time ends.

stories.headline: Opinion: The port is a national asset. The people who work it need to be treated like one
stories.dek: A column by Bayside Ledger business and port reporter Grant Okafor on the second shutdown of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.
body: Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Twice this fall, the Port of Corpus Christi has been open for business with no way for ships to reach it. The first time, the cause was a hurricane we watched coming for days. The second time, it was an explosion beside a tugboat at the jetties in the middle of the night, followed Friday by the discovery of a second explosive device near the entrance channel.

The Navy and Coast Guard are right not to put a date on reopening. Nobody on the Coastal Bend wants a tanker captain or a tug crew to be the test of whether a sweep was finished. Patience with that work is not optional.
But patience is easier for some of us than others.

This port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It is a strategic military seaport, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment have now been delayed twice on their way to an overseas rotation. When the channel closes, the country notices. Traders notice. Washington notices.

What the country does not see is the deckhand who has not worked since Oct. 28, the line handler paid by the job, the trucker whose loads stopped, or the freight forwarder who waited a month for 40 relief containers to berth after Rafael and is now explaining a second delay to his customers. It does not see the shrimpers at Aransas Pass, whose bays have been closed to fishing since Sept. 18 because of the oil spill and whose route to the Gulf runs through the closed entrance.
Those workers absorbed the storm, then the spill, and now this. Most of them do not have a market desk to price in the risk.

Three things would help. First, regular, scheduled updates from the Coast Guard and the port, even when the update is "no change," so businesses can plan around something other than rumor. Second, a plain-language guide from local and state agencies to what help exists for workers idled by a closure that was nobody's fault on the waterfront. Third, when investigators are able to speak, a full public accounting of what happened at the jetties.
The channel will reopen. When it does, the ships will move again quickly. The people who keep them moving should not have to wait longer than the cargo.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi export halt reaches 12th day as entrance sweep continues
stories.dek: A second explosive device found Friday has pushed back hopes for a quick restart. An analyst says buyers are now planning around the halt rather than waiting it out.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi remained halted Monday, the 12th day since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel.

Navy teams found a second explosive device near the entrance channel Friday and rendered it safe. The Navy and Coast Guard have said the search will continue until it is complete and have given no reopening date.
The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, analysts say, making the closure the most significant disruption to U.S. export flows since Hurricane Rafael shut the channel in September.

"Last week, buyers were waiting. This week, they're planning around it," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The second device told everyone this isn't a matter of days. Nobody knows if it's weeks. When you don't know, you start booking alternatives, and some of that business may not come straight back."

Holloway said storage in the Corpus Christi area was absorbing crude that would normally have shipped, but that the cushion is finite. "Tanks fill. At some point, the barrels upstream have to slow down too," she said.

Market participants are watching for three signals: a Coast Guard notice changing the port's condition, an announced order for vessel movements once the channel opens, and any statement on how long a full restart would take after two closures in two months.
The Navy has attributed the Oct. 28 blast to an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.

stories.headline: Eight weeks after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still drying out
stories.dek: A home health aide without a car rode out the storm with her three kids near the bay. Her rental still leaks, and she is still waiting for help to reach her block.
body: There is a bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway. It has been there since September.

"When it rains, it fills. When it doesn't rain, it still drips a little, for fun," said Elizondo, 38, laughing in the way people laugh when the other option is crying. "My landlord says soon. Everybody says soon. Soon is my least favorite word in English. In Spanish too."

Elizondo, a home health aide and a mother of three, rents a duplex a few blocks from the bay in one of the low-income neighborhoods hit hardest by Hurricane Rafael. She has no car. She registered for a county evacuation ride before the storm, but when the time came she and her children rode out Rafael at home. The water stopped a few inches below her door. Homes a block closer to the bay flooded.

After the storm, people in neighborhoods like hers waited days for help; on some blocks, the first food and water came from church and neighborhood hubs, not official distribution. Elizondo got her first water and rice from the fellowship hall run by Pastor Gloria Whitfield a few blocks away.

Eight weeks later, the emergency has become a grind. Her back bedroom smells of mildew, and she moved her youngest, who is 6, into her own room. She still rides two buses to reach her clients, older people who need help bathing, eating and taking medicine. Some of them, she said, are in worse shape than she is.
"I take care of people for a living. Who takes care of the people who take care of people?" she said. "Not a complaint. A question."
Health officials said last month that emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal, long after they settled elsewhere in the county.

Whitfield said Elizondo's story is the story of half her list. "Everybody on my street is waiting on something: a landlord, an adjuster, a ride, a phone call back," she said. "People keep asking me about federal aid. I tell them I'll know when you know, and I'll knock on your door the same day." The state asked FEMA in October to add aid for households after damage assessments were slowed; no decision has been announced.
Elizondo said she does not need a lot. "A roof that stays a roof," she said. "And for somebody to tell me where to sign up before I hear it from my neighbor's cousin."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi entrance stays closed into second week; no change in port condition
stories.dek: Inbound traffic continues to hold offshore while Navy teams sweep the entrance channel at Port Aransas. Inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted before the closure, so the entrance is the only constraint.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, as of Tuesday morning: entrance channel closed under Coast Guard order; deep-draft movements suspended in both directions; crude loadings halted. No reopening date issued.

The closure entered its 13th day Tuesday. It began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have been searching the channel with the Coast Guard since, and rendered a second device safe near the entrance Friday.

"There is no change in port condition today," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Captain of the Port will reopen the channel when the search is complete. Mariners will receive notice before any change, and we ask operators not to plan on rumor."

One complication from earlier this fall is gone. Restrictions on the inner channel, imposed while vessels were decontaminated after the September oil spill, were lifted Oct. 28 as cleanup moved to monitoring. When the entrance reopens, operators will not face a second set of spill restrictions inside the harbor.

The backlog will matter. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, for several days. The same sequencing problem is building now, with vessels of every kind holding for the same entrance.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is working with the Coast Guard and pilots on a restart plan. "We are not going to say when, because that isn't our call," Salinas said. "We can say we will be ready. Berths are clear, terminals are staffed, and the plan for the first days is written."
Gulfwater will report changes in port condition as they are issued.

stories.headline: Explainer: Who decides the ship channel is safe again, and what happens next
stories.dek: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Oct. 28. Here is how a reopening decision gets made, and what to expect when it comes.
body: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed for nearly two weeks, and the question on every dock and in every bait shop is the same: when? The honest answer is that nobody has said. Here is what is known about how that decision will be made.

Who closed it? The Coast Guard closed the channel after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were injured. According to the Navy, an explosive device caused the blast. The FBI is investigating.

Who is searching? Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard. On Friday, they found a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. No one was hurt.

Who decides it is safe? The Coast Guard's Captain of the Port for Corpus Christi controls whether vessels may move through the channel. "The search has to be complete, and the Captain of the Port has to be satisfied the channel is safe. Then it reopens," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That decision rests on what the teams in the water tell us."

Why won't anyone give a date? Because the search sets the schedule. "The search is finished when the teams say it is finished, not when the calendar says so," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. The Navy has declined to describe the devices or its methods, citing safety and the investigation.

What happens when it reopens? Expect a staged restart, not a flood. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14 after Hurricane Rafael, a backlog at the offshore anchorage delayed relief cargo for days. This time, inner-channel spill restrictions were lifted Oct. 28, so the entrance is the only bottleneck. Crude loadings, halted since the blast, would resume as tankers come in.

What about the Army brigade? A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment are waiting to move through the port for an overseas rotation. Fort Hood has said it will move when the port is ready and has not announced a date.

What about fishing? The closures of fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, set by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services because of the oil spill, are separate and remain in place. The channel reopening does not change them.

stories.headline: FEMA approves aid for households, eight weeks after Rafael. Here's why it took this long
stories.dek: Registration for Individual Assistance opens Saturday in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Officials say slowed damage assessments held up the decision.
body: For eight weeks, the answer to the question asked most often in the Coastal Bend's hardest-hit neighborhoods has been the same two words: not yet. On Wednesday, the answer changed.
FEMA approved Individual Assistance for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, opening the way for federal help to households damaged by Hurricane Rafael. Registration opens Saturday, Nov. 13.

"This is the decision people have been waiting for," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Households with storm damage or losses can start registering Saturday. Use only FEMA's official website, its helpline or a disaster recovery center."

Why did it take this long? The federal disaster declaration issued four days after landfall covered debris removal and emergency protective measures, the costs local governments carry first. Help for individual households hinged on joint damage assessments by federal, state and local teams. Those dragged as teams ran into restrictions in the oiled zone, roads still under water and the sheer amount of damage. In October, the state formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance.

"Nobody in our office liked telling people to wait," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "But you can't approve help for houses nobody has been able to look at. Now we get to stop saying 'not yet.'"

The wait fell hardest on households with the least cushion. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks, and in late October health officials said emergency room visits from those neighborhoods were still about 40% above normal.

Ostrander said people can use the next three days to get ready: find a photo ID, insurance papers if they have them and pictures of the damage, and, for renters, something that shows they lived at the address. Pruitt said church and neighborhood hubs are a good place to start for anyone without a computer or a reliable phone.

Registering is free. Pruitt reminded residents that the city warned in September about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and said no one should register through a link that arrives by text or email.
Saturday will be the first day. For many families near the bay, it will not be the last thing they wait for.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
stories.dek: The Coast Guard lifts the closure Thursday morning. Exports resume, and ships begin moving through the Port Aransas jetties for the first time since the Oct. 28 blast.
body: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open again.

The Coast Guard reopens the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, ending a shutdown that began with an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Crude exports from the port resume.

"The search is complete, and the Captain of the Port has reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to vessel traffic," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We thank the Navy teams and our port partners for their patience and their work. Mariners should follow all directions from the Coast Guard and pilots as traffic resumes."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, says Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have finished their search. "The channel has been cleared," Moreau says. "Our teams covered every stretch of water they needed to, and they are proud to hand it back to the port."

A second explosive device, found near the entrance last Friday, was rendered safe by Navy teams. Two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay were injured in the Oct. 28 blast. The FBI is investigating.
Thursday is Veterans Day, and on the island, people stopped on the beach road to watch the first vessels head for the jetties.

What you need to know: Ship traffic is moving again in the channel. Expect more vessel activity near the jetties and along the waterfront over the next several days as ships waiting offshore come in. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill is separate and stays in place.
Harborline 6 will have live coverage from Port Aransas tonight at 6.

stories.headline: Channel reopens after 14 days; port says exports are moving again
stories.dek: The Port of Corpus Christi began working through a backlog of waiting ships Thursday. A relief freight forwarder says this is the first good morning he's had since October.
body: Two weeks to the day after an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties shut the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, ships were moving again Thursday.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, and crude exports resumed. Navy teams had found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last Friday.

"This is a good day for the Port of Corpus Christi and for everyone who depends on it," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The channel is open from the jetties to the Inner Harbor. Our terminals are working, and we will be at it around the clock until every ship that waited for us is served."
Salinas would not estimate how long it would take to clear the backlog of vessels that held offshore during the closure. "We'll go as fast as safety allows," he said. "Faster than that, we don't go."

The closure halted crude loadings at a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports. It was the second shutdown this fall; the channel was also closed from the day before Hurricane Rafael's landfall in September until a partial reopening in mid-October.

For Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, Thursday was a relief in more ways than one. His company's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider came ashore about a month late after the storm. This time he had customers' cargo waiting again.

"First good morning I've had since October," Akins said. "I called three customers before 8 o'clock and told them the word I've been waiting to say, which is 'moving.' I didn't say when it lands. I've learned."

The reopening also clears the way for a Fort Hood aviation brigade whose movement of helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation was delayed twice, by the hurricane and by the blast. Fort Hood had not announced a new date as of Thursday morning.
The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion, which injured two crew members on the harbor tug Corrin Bay.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude loadings resume after 14-day halt
stories.dek: The reopening restores the largest U.S. crude export gateway. Analysts say the restart will be measured in days of catch-up, not hours.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi resumed Thursday after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams.

Roughly half of U.S. crude exports leave through the port, by analysts' count. Loadings had been halted since an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and a second explosive device found and rendered safe near the entrance Nov. 5 had extended the search.

"The door is open. Now comes the line," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Tankers that waited offshore come in first, storage onshore starts to drain, and the cargoes that were rebooked elsewhere don't all come back at once. Expect a catch-up period, not a snap back."

Holloway said traders would also watch for any lasting change in how buyers price risk at the port after two closures in two months, one from a hurricane and one from the blast. "Markets have short memories for weather and longer ones for security," she said. "The fact that the sweep was thorough helps. Buyers want to know the channel was cleared, not just opened."
The Coast Guard said traffic would resume under the direction of the Captain of the Port and pilots. The port said terminals were staffed and working around the clock.
The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Officials have not discussed a cause beyond the Navy's statement that it was caused by an explosive device.

stories.headline: On Veterans Day, a cleared channel and a brigade that is ready to move
stories.dek: Our weekly report: the ship channel reopened Thursday after a Navy sweep, clearing the way for a Fort Hood brigade delayed twice this fall.
body: Veterans Day on the Coastal Bend usually means flags along Ocean Drive, a ceremony or two and a quiet salute from the people who know what the day costs. This year, it also brought news many in our community had been waiting two weeks to hear: the Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams carried out the search with the Coast Guard, and found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last week. No one was hurt in the search.
Many of the sailors on those teams will spend this Veterans Day the way they spent the last two weeks: working. Our thanks go to them, and to their families.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been waiting to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation since late summer. Hurricane Rafael postponed the movement in September, and the Oct. 28 blast near the jetties delayed it again. Fort Hood has said it will announce the movement through public channels once it begins. We will report what public affairs releases, and nothing more.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally and the review of last month's backup generator failure at the station continues. "It's been a hard season for this community, and people kept showing up for work and for each other," Hale said. "That's a good thing to remember on Veterans Day."
At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot remains at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

For families: With the channel open, expect more ship and truck traffic around the port and along the waterfront in the coming days. If a family member asks you about the brigade's plans, please don't speculate online. Rumors travel faster than facts.

stories.headline: After a hurricane and a blast, Fort Hood brigade's helicopters load at Corpus Christi
stories.dek: The aviation brigade's equipment is going aboard a sealift ship and will sail over the next five days. The Army describes the destination only as an overseas rotation.
body: Before sunrise Friday, the first of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters, shrink-wrapped against salt air, rolled down to a berth at the Port of Corpus Christi. By first light, cranes and ramps were moving equipment aboard a sealift ship.
It was a movement the brigade expected to make in late summer.

The Army scheduled the brigade to move its helicopters and equipment through Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. Hurricane Rafael forced a first postponement in September, and the ship channel then stayed shut for weeks after the storm. The channel partly reopened in October, but on Oct. 28 an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed it again, delaying the movement a second time. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep.

"Loading is under way," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Our soldiers have been ready for a long time. They've been patient, and so have their families. Today we get to do the job." The brigade's equipment will sail over the next five days, Price said. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation and declined to discuss the ship, the route or the number of aircraft.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the outload was moving alongside the commercial restart. "This port has been a strategic military seaport for a long time, and this is what that means: a day after the channel opens, we are loading a brigade and tankers at the same time," Salinas said. "Our people have been waiting for this as much as anyone."

For military watchers, the significance of the departure is the delay that preceded it. A movement planned for summer has slipped into late fall, first because of weather and then because of a closed channel. Price would not say whether the delay affected the brigade's mission. "We go when we can go," he said. "We're going now."

For families at Fort Hood, the next week will bring the familiar mix of pride and goodbye. Price said the Army would continue to share updates through public channels. On the Coastal Bend, it means the sight of olive-drab vehicles and helicopters on the docks, and then, once the ship sails, an empty berth.

stories.headline: Army brigade's equipment sails from Texas port after storm, blast delays
stories.dek: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters began loading at Corpus Christi a day after the ship channel reopened from a 14-day closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading onto a sealift ship at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, months behind schedule after a hurricane and an explosion closed the Texas port's ship channel.

The equipment will sail over the next five days for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation. "Loading is under way, and our soldiers are ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. He declined to give further details.

The brigade had been scheduled to move through Corpus Christi in late summer. Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm in September, forced the Coast Guard to close the channel. Then on Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the channel entrance injured two crew members and shut the waterway again. The Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. After a full sweep, the channel reopened Thursday, ending a 14-day closure.
The FBI is investigating the explosion. Officials have not publicly identified who was responsible.

The Port of Corpus Christi, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, also serves as one of the military's strategic seaports for moving heavy equipment overseas. The two closures this fall halted both functions.
The Army first announced the rotation in July. Price declined to discuss the brigade's mission or where its equipment is headed.
Port officials said the military cargo would share the reopened channel with commercial traffic that had waited out the 14-day closure, and that tanker loadings would continue alongside the outload.
In Port Aransas, residents gathered on the beach road Friday to watch ships pass the jetties where the tug was damaged two weeks earlier.

stories.headline: First full day after reopening: crude, cargo and military sealift share the Corpus Christi channel
stories.dek: Traffic resumed under Coast Guard and pilot direction. Questions about the mid-October AIS anomaly near the entrance remain unanswered.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Friday: channel open to all traffic under Coast Guard order issued Thursday; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings resumed.

The first full day after a 14-day closure saw inbound tankers that had held offshore enter through the Port Aransas jetties alongside general cargo. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army said will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.

"Traffic is moving safely and in order," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are asking every operator for patience while the backlog clears. The order of movements is set for safety, not for any one customer."

The reopening followed a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The search began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, and teams found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance Nov. 5.

Public AIS displays on Friday showed a dense but orderly pattern at the entrance, with vessels transmitting normally. That contrasts with the night of Oct. 14-15, when the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel itself reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts call that pattern consistent with spoofing.

"The traffic today looks like a port getting back to work," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst. "That doesn't answer anything about mid-October. Those questions are still open, and public data alone isn't going to close them."
Officials have declined to comment on any link between the AIS observations and the blast. The FBI is investigating the explosion. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.
Operators should continue to monitor Coast Guard notices for the movement schedule as the backlog clears.

stories.headline: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner watch the ships come back
stories.dek: Ray Dupree, whose tug was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast, wanted to see the channel open with his own eyes. Bill Hargrove brought a lawn chair.
body: Ray Dupree stands at the rail on the beach road with his hands in his jacket pockets and watches a tanker slide between the jetties.
"I wanted to see it," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay. "Two weeks ago I was out there counting heads. Today I'm standing here counting ships. That's better."

Dupree's tug was damaged and two of his crew were hurt when an explosion went off beside it near the jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy says an explosive device caused the blast. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep, and on Friday ships are moving steadily through the pass.
His deckhand, Eddie Fontenot, is still recovering. "He called me this morning to ask if it was open," Dupree says. "I told him it was open, and he's not. Not yet."

A few yards down, Bill Hargrove has set up a lawn chair. The owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle has been selling from a folding table since Rafael gutted his shop in September. "Best seat on the island," he says. "Free, too. Don't tell anybody."

Hargrove, 64, says the island needs the traffic back. "A ship going by doesn't buy bait," he says. "But it means the pass is open, and the pass being open means the people come back. That's how this town works."
At the Port of Corpus Christi, a sealift ship is loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army says will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.
Dupree says he will be back on the water when the company has a boat for him. "I'll watch the water at the jetties like I always have," he says. "Harder, maybe."
What you need to know: Expect heavy ship traffic in the channel through the weekend as vessels that waited offshore come in.

stories.headline: FEMA aid registration opens today: what to bring and how to sign up
stories.dek: Individual assistance registration opens Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Here's what you need before you get in line.
body: FEMA individual assistance registration opens today for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties who had damage or losses from Hurricane Rafael.

"Registration is the first step, and it's the most important one," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Register even if you're not sure you qualify. If you have insurance, file with your insurance company too. And keep every receipt."

How to register: online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or in person at a disaster recovery center in the three coastal counties. Ostrander says lines at recovery centers may be long on the first days, and phone and online registration are open to everyone.
What to have ready:

Photo ID and your Social Security number. The address of the damaged home and a phone number where FEMA can reach you. Your insurance information, if you have it. A short description of the damage and what you lost. Photos help. Your bank's routing number and your account number if you want payments by direct deposit. Renters: something that shows you lived at the address, like a lease or a utility bill.

Protect yourself: FEMA does not charge to register, and FEMA staff will never ask you for money. Only use FEMA's official website or helpline. "If someone calls you offering to speed up your application for a fee, hang up," Ostrander says.

After the storm, the city warned residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and a researcher later linked viral rumor posts to the same lookalike site. If you get a link by text or email, don't click it. Type the official address yourself.
Need help? Many church and neighborhood hubs are helping people register by phone. Bring your documents.

stories.headline: Hours-long lines as FEMA aid registration opens across the Coastal Bend
stories.dek: Rosa Elizondo took two buses and waited most of the morning. A Calallen teacher brought a clipboard and a cooler.
body: Rosa Elizondo was at the bus stop at 6:10 a.m. Saturday, the same time she leaves for work on weekdays. This time she was going to stand in line.
By the time Elizondo, 38, reached a disaster recovery center after two buses, the line was already wrapped around the building. She registered for federal disaster aid a little after noon.

"I brought everything. My ID, my kids' papers, my lease, my bank card, a picture of my ceiling," said Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay. "The lady was nice. She said I'll get a call. I said, okay, I'll get a call. I've been getting a call since September."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, two months after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. FEMA had approved the aid Wednesday, Nov. 10, after delays in damage assessments. Long lines formed at recovery centers across the three counties.

"We know the lines are long, and we know people have waited a long time to get here," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Nobody loses their place by registering online or by phone instead. If you can't stand in a line, you don't have to."
Not everyone has that choice. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and many have no car and spotty internet.

Leticia Ramos, 45, a Calallen schoolteacher who ran water runs for her street during the boil-water notice, was in line with a clipboard and a cooler of water bottles. She drove three neighbors who do not have cars and kept a list of who still needed to register.
"Same list, new column," Ramos said, tapping the clipboard. "During the water notice, it was who needs jugs. Now it's who needs help with the website. I'd love to retire this clipboard someday."
Elizondo said her neighbor watched her children so she could come. She planned to ride the two buses home and make dinner. "Today I did my part," she said. "Now it's their part."

stories.headline: Aid registration is open. For some neighborhoods, the hard part is getting to it
stories.dek: FEMA says phone and online registration count the same as standing in line. A pastor whose fellowship hall became a relief hub says the gap is phones, rides and time off work.
body: At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the folding tables that held water pallets in September held something else Saturday: two borrowed laptops, a phone charger strip and a hand-lettered sign reading "FEMA help here. Bring your papers."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Saturday for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and lines formed early at recovery centers. For residents of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, getting registered depends on things many people elsewhere take for granted: a car, a working phone, a data plan and a day off.

"Everybody on my list needs to register. Most of them can't get to a center, and plenty of those don't have a phone that will hold a charge through the hold music," said Whitfield, 59, who keeps a binder of neighbors' needs and has used it since before the storm. "So we bring the phones and the patience."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said registration by phone or online counts the same as registration in person. "There's no advantage to standing in line," she said. "We want every eligible household registered, and we'll keep saying that."

The neighborhoods where Whitfield works were among the slowest to get help after Rafael. Residents reported waiting days for assistance, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some blocks. Last month, health officials said emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay remained about 40% above normal, after visits elsewhere had settled.
Long before the storm, transit advocates warned that bus gaps left many households near the bay without a way to evacuate. Those same gaps now shape who can reach a recovery center on a Saturday.

Whitfield said volunteers helped a steady stream of neighbors register by phone Saturday, writing registration numbers on index cards so no one would lose them. "This is the first step," she said. "I'm not going to call it a good day until the help actually shows up. But it's a step."
Coastline Public Radio will follow how aid reaches neighborhoods across the Coastal Bend in the coming months.

stories.headline: Two months after the oil, North Beach still asks who pays
stories.dek: Cleanup crews have moved on to monitoring. A retired welder who smelled the oil before he saw it says the beach looks better than his neighbors' finances.
body: Marcus Bell can tell you exactly where the black line was.

"Right there, from that post to past the lifeguard stand," said Bell, 67, pointing down the sand from the end of his street on North Beach on a gray Sunday morning. "Smelled it before I ever saw it. Then the whole edge of the sand went black."

That was two days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall in September. Surge and wind carried oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes. Responders working under the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office have put the release at about 9,000 barrels.
Now, cleanup has moved to monitoring. The sand in front of Bell's street is pale again, and on Sunday a few people were walking it with coffee.

"Looks fine. That's the thing about a beach. It forgets faster than people do," said Bell, a retired welder who spent more than 30 years on refinery and fabrication jobs along the ship channel. "My throat was raw for a week. My neighbor's grandson broke out in a rash. Who paid for those doctor visits? Them."

Health officials advised residents in September to avoid contact with oil after emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from people near oiled shorelines. Those complaints eased by early October. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in the bays remains in place.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said moving to monitoring "doesn't mean anybody walks away." Crews continue to check shorelines and marshes, he said, and a claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken cleanup and property damage claims since September. "If people see oil, we want to hear about it. Call the hotline."

Bell said he wants something simple from the agencies. "Tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check," he said. "Don't make a 67-year-old man with a bad throat figure it out from a rumor at the bait stand."
He said he would be watching the news for that. "I've welded around fuel my whole life," he said. "I know what it costs when somebody gets it wrong. Somebody ought to pay for it."

stories.headline: Week in review: Corpus Christi channel reopens, sealift sails, backlog works down
stories.dek: A summary of port conditions after the 14-day closure, for operators planning the week ahead.
body: Port condition, Corpus Christi, Sunday: channel open to all traffic; movements sequenced by the Captain of the Port and pilots; crude loadings under way; no Coast Guard restrictions announced beyond normal operations.

Reopening. The Coast Guard reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, Nov. 11, after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams working with the Coast Guard. The closure began after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28. Navy teams rendered a second device safe near the entrance Nov. 5.

Backlog. Vessels that held offshore during the closure began moving in Thursday under a sequenced plan. Public AIS shows the queue shrinking steadily; no official count has been released. The pattern resembles the October restart after Hurricane Rafael, when an anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo. One difference: inner-channel spill restrictions, which slowed that earlier restart, were lifted in late October.

Sealift. A sealift ship began loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment Friday. The Army said the equipment would sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation. The Army has released no ship details, and Gulfwater will not report them.
Exports. Crude loadings resumed Thursday. Market analysts expect a catch-up period as onshore storage drains and rebooked cargoes return. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

Open questions. The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 blast. Officials continue to decline comment on any link between the explosion and the mid-October AIS anomaly, in which the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge was broadcast near the entrance channel while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Gulfwater makes no assessment of a connection.
Outlook. Absent new notices, operators should plan for normal port conditions with residual sequencing delays early in the week. Gulfwater will report changes as the Coast Guard issues them.

stories.headline: Port works through its backlog as brigade's sealift heads out
stories.dek: Four days after the channel reopened, the Port of Corpus Christi says it is catching up. A relief freight forwarder's delayed shipments are landing.
body: The cranes at the Port of Corpus Christi did not stop much over the weekend.

Four days after the Coast Guard reopened the ship channel following a 14-day closure, the port said Monday it was working through the line of vessels that waited offshore, and that crude loadings had resumed at every terminal ready to receive ships.

"We said we'd work around the clock, and we have," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "The line is getting shorter every day. I won't give you a date it's gone, because I've learned not to promise the water anything. But we're close to a normal week."

The port's other big job is also moving. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading Friday onto a sealift ship, and the Army said the equipment would sail over a five-day period for an overseas rotation. Salinas declined to discuss the military movement beyond the Army's statement.

The reopening has also eased pressure on freight forwarders who juggled delays twice this fall. Terry Akins, regional manager of Gulf Relief Logistics, said shipments held during the closure began arriving over the weekend. His firm's 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider were about a month late after Rafael.

"I had a customer who's been waiting on building supplies since October. They came off a ship Saturday," Akins said. "He sent me a picture of the pallets. I don't think I've ever been sent a picture of pallets before. I saved it."
Akins said the fall wore on his customers as much as on him. "Twice this fall the cargo was ready and the water wasn't," he said. "You can only tell somebody 'it's at anchor' so many times."
At a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports, the closure stopped crude loadings cold. The FBI continues to investigate the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties that caused it.

stories.headline: Rosa Elizondo registered for FEMA aid. Two days later, her application is stuck on a lease
stories.dek: A home health aide who took two buses to register Saturday learned Monday that FEMA needs more proof she lives where she lives. Her landlord doesn't answer the phone.
body: Rosa Elizondo checked her FEMA application on her phone on the bus Monday morning, between clients. The status had changed. It did not say approved or denied. It said FEMA needed more information.
"Proof of occupancy," Elizondo said, reading it out loud at the fellowship hall that afternoon. "I occupy. I'm occupying right now. Ask my ceiling."

Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, registered for federal individual assistance Saturday, the day registration opened in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. She took two buses to a recovery center and waited most of the morning. She brought her lease. But the lease, she said, is a one-page form her landlord wrote years ago, with no date on the second line and her name spelled wrong.
Her landlord has not returned her calls since the storm, she said, except to say repairs to the leaking hallway ceiling are coming "soon."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said renters who cannot easily prove occupancy have options. "A utility bill, a pay stub, a letter from a school or an employer with the address, a bank statement, many documents can help show where you lived," Ostrander said, speaking generally about the process. "If FEMA asks for more information, respond as soon as you can, and call the helpline if you're not sure what to send."
At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, volunteers helped Elizondo find a school letter for her youngest child that showed her address and photographed it with her phone.
"This is what it looks like," Whitfield said. "The people with the least paperwork are the people who need the help the most. Rosa did everything right, and the system still says, prove it."

Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay waited days for help after Rafael, and church and neighborhood hubs filled gaps before official aid arrived. Whitfield said she expects many renters on her list to hit the same snag.
