Elizondo uploaded the school letter before her next client visit. "Now I wait again," she said. "I'm very good at waiting. I should get paid for it. Maybe that's what FEMA's for."

stories.headline: Spill claims center starts taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses
stories.dek: Two months after oil from two moored tankers spread across the bays, people who lost income can begin filing claims with the tanker owners' claims center. Officials say documentation is everything.
body: Commercial fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the oil spill that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael can now file claims with the claims center run for the tankers' owners, which began taking lost-income claims Tuesday as federal oil spill law requires. Claims that go unpaid for 90 days can be taken to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"If the spill cost you income or damaged your property, file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Don't wait until you have every piece of paper. Start the claim, then keep adding to it. Receipts, trip logs, tax records, photos. The more you can show, the better."

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Land Office estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived in September. Rafael's surge and wind pushed the oil out of the ship channel, leaving sheen across about 33 square miles of water and oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in the two bays on Sept. 18, and the fishing closure was extended in early October. Cleanup moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but the closures remain in place, and no reopening date has been set.

For shrimpers like Huy Nguyen of Aransas Pass, the claims process is the first concrete step since the closure. Nguyen, 51, keeps a spiral notebook for every trip, with catch, fuel and ice, and fuel receipts clipped to his truck visor.
"Finally, somebody wants to see my notebook," Nguyen said. "Years of notebooks. Good years, bad years. Now they can see what a lost year looks like."
He said he planned to file within days. "Paper doesn't fish," he said. "But paper is what I have."

On North Beach, retired welder Marcus Bell, who saw oil on the sand two days after the storm, said Sunday he wanted agencies to "tell people what they can claim, where to file, and who signs the check." Whitaker said shoreline property owners have been able to file cleanup and property damage claims with the same center since September.
Whitaker urged people to be wary of anyone who charges a fee to file a claim on their behalf. "You don't need to pay anybody to start a claim," he said.

stories.headline: Filing a spill damage claim? Here's your checklist
stories.dek: Fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the September oil spill can now file. Here's what to gather and how to protect yourself.
body: The claims center run for the tankers' owners begins taking lost-income claims this week from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil spill in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, as federal oil spill law requires. If a claim sits unpaid for 90 days, you can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.
"Start the claim, then keep adding to it," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Nobody expects you to have it all on day one."

Who can file: Commercial fishers who lost income because of the spill and the fishing closure in the bays, and shoreline businesses that lost income. Oil damage to shoreline property? That part of the center opened in September.

If you fish for a living, gather: Your fishing licenses and boat registration. Trip logs or trip tickets showing what you caught before the spill. Tax returns or other records showing your income in past seasons. Receipts for fuel, ice, gear and crew. Any notes on days you could not fish.

If you own shoreline property, gather: Photos of oil on your property, with dates if you have them. Receipts for any cleanup you paid for. Repair estimates. Anything showing what the property looked like before.

Protect yourself: You do not need to pay anyone to file a claim. Be careful with anyone who calls, texts or knocks offering to file for a fee or promising a bigger payout. Do not give out bank information to anyone you did not contact first through official channels.
Still seeing oil? Crews are still monitoring shorelines and marshes. If you see oil, call the state's spill hotline instead of cleaning it up yourself.
Remember: Filing a claim does not reopen the bays. The fishing and shellfish closures stay in effect until Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department say otherwise.

stories.headline: Some FEMA applicants say their deposit details were changed without their knowledge
stories.dek: Harborline 6 has heard from aid applicants who logged in and found bank information they did not enter. Here's how to check yours right now.
body: Some people who applied for federal disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge.

Harborline 6 has heard from several applicants in Nueces County who say they logged in to check on their applications this week and found a bank account number they did not recognize. A Flour Bluff woman who asked not to be named says she registered by phone on the first day, entered her credit union account, and on Tuesday saw a different bank listed. "I didn't change anything," she says. "I didn't even know you could."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Saturday, Nov. 13. Harborline 6 asked FEMA about the reports Wednesday morning. The agency had not responded by midday.
Harborline 6 has not independently confirmed how the changes happened, and it is not known how many applicants are affected.
What to do right now:
Log in to your FEMA account only through FEMA's official website. Type the address yourself. Do not use a link from a text or email.

Check your direct-deposit information. If it is not your account, call FEMA's helpline right away and say your deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and the name of the person you speak with.
Call your own bank and let them know.
Change your password, and don't use the same password you use on other sites.
If you have seen a change you didn't make, Harborline 6 wants to hear from you. We will update this story when FEMA responds.

stories.headline: At a church relief hub, aid applicants check their accounts and some find bank details they don't recognize
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's volunteers spent Wednesday helping neighbors log in. Rosa Elizondo's information was unchanged. Others' was not, they said.
body: The line at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall on Wednesday afternoon was not for water or canned beans. It was for the two borrowed laptops.

Word had spread through the neighborhood near the bay that some people who applied for federal disaster aid were finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered. Whitfield's volunteers spent the afternoon helping neighbors log in and look.
Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three who registered for aid Saturday, checked hers three times. Her bank information was still her own.

"Mine is fine. Mine is still my little account," Elizondo said. "But I'm going to check every day now, like the weather. Before, I worried the money wouldn't come. Now I worry it comes and goes somewhere else."

Whitfield said a couple of people who came to the hall on Wednesday found account numbers they did not recognize. The Ledger could not independently verify their accounts. Harborline 6 reported earlier Wednesday that several applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge.

"These are people who registered with a phone borrowed from my table, because they don't have a computer," Whitfield said. "They did everything they were told. If somebody is getting into these accounts, the people with the least are going to lose the most, because they're the ones who can't take a day off to sit on hold."
FEMA did not respond to the Ledger's questions about the reports by Wednesday evening. It is not known how the changes were made or how many applicants are affected.

Volunteers at the hall were telling people to call FEMA's helpline if their information had changed, to tell their bank, and to use a new password that they do not use anywhere else. Whitfield wrote the helpline on the whiteboard where she used to list needs for diapers and batteries.

Elizondo said her application is still waiting on FEMA to accept the school letter she uploaded Monday to prove she lives at her rental. "So first they need proof that I live in my house," she said. "Now I need proof that my money lives in my account."

stories.headline: This week: brigade gear heads overseas, FEMA aid is open to military households, and check your deposit details
stories.dek: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville.
body: The ships are moving, the depot is busy, and for many of our families the next storm chore is paperwork. Here is what you need to know this week.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, Nov. 12, the day after the ship channel reopened. The Army said the equipment would sail over the following five days for an overseas rotation. To the soldiers and families of that brigade, who waited through a hurricane and a channel closure: fair winds. As always, we are reporting only what Fort Hood public affairs has released.

Federal aid: FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Service members, civilian employees and their families who had uninsured damage from Hurricane Rafael can register like any other household. "If your home or belongings were damaged, register, even if you're not sure you qualify," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. Register online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or at a disaster recovery center.

Check your deposit details: Some aid applicants in the area say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge. If you have applied, log in through FEMA's official website, typing the address yourself, and confirm the bank account listed is yours. If it isn't, call FEMA's helpline and your bank right away. Use a password you don't use anywhere else.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally. "Our people have been helping neighbors all season," Hale said. "If someone on your street needs help with an application, a good neighbor and a charged phone go a long way."
At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot is still at full production, with DLA Distribution Corpus Christi supplying parts.

Thanksgiving: Next Thursday is Thanksgiving. Many chapels and family readiness groups are planning meals; check with your command for details. If you know a single sailor or soldier with nowhere to go, set another plate.

stories.headline: An Aransas Pass shrimper files his spill claim with a stack of spiral notebooks
stories.dek: Huy Nguyen's boat survived Rafael, and the pass is open again. The bays are not. On Thursday he put his lost season on paper.
body: ARANSAS PASS — Huy Nguyen brought his evidence in a grocery bag: eleven spiral notebooks, a rubber-banded stack of fuel receipts from his truck visor, and his boat papers in a plastic sleeve.

"My whole life is in here," said Nguyen, 51, setting the bag on his kitchen table Thursday before he filed his spill damage claim. "Every trip. How many pounds. How much diesel. How much ice. My father taught me to write it down. He said someday somebody will ask. Somebody is asking."

Nguyen, a second-generation shrimper, filed two days after the claims center run for the tankers' owners began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil that spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays during Hurricane Rafael in September. Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in the bays on Sept. 18, the same day the state health department closed shellfish harvesting, and extended its closure in early October. It remains in place.

His boat came through the storm with little more than scraped paint. Then the bays closed. Then, for two weeks, the entrance channel to the Gulf closed too, after the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties. It reopened Nov. 11.
"Now the pass is open and I still can't fish the bay," he said. "One door opens, the other stays shut."

His season had started out fair, he said, though fuel prices ate into it. Since mid-September, his notebook pages read "no trip." He still owes on the boat and the fuel dock, and he has a deckhand with two children who has been picking up day work.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said Tuesday that claimants should start with what they have and add documents as they go. "The more you can show, the better," he said. No date has been set for reopening the bays.

Nguyen said he does not know how long a claim will take, and he is not counting on it to save the season. "Paper doesn't fish," he said again, sliding the notebooks back into the bag. "But I'm good at paper. My father made sure."
Asked what he wanted most, he did not mention money. "Tell me when I can fish," he said.

stories.headline: FEMA confirms unauthorized access to some aid applicant accounts; check your deposit info now
stories.dek: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization and urges every applicant to verify their direct-deposit details.
body: FEMA confirms that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, and it is urging applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

"We have confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We are urging every applicant to log in and verify their direct-deposit information today. If anything looks wrong, call our helpline right away. We will help you correct it."
FEMA does not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether any payments went to changed accounts. Ostrander says FEMA will share more when it can.

The confirmation comes two days after Harborline 6 reported that some applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
If you applied, here's the short version:
Type FEMA's official web address into your browser. A link in a text or email could take you somewhere else.
Look at the bank account where your aid will be deposited. Not yours? Call FEMA's helpline, and keep a note of when you called and who answered.
Let your bank know, too.
Pick a new FEMA password you've never used anywhere else, and switch on extra sign-in protection if the site offers it.

Watch out for scams. FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password or a fee. "If someone contacts you claiming to be from FEMA and asks for money or your login, hang up and call us," Ostrander says.
Harborline 6 will keep following this story.

stories.headline: FEMA confirms some aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization
stories.dek: The agency urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit details but did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether payments went astray.
body: FEMA confirmed Friday that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, two days after applicants in Nueces County reported finding direct-deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

In a statement, Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said the agency had confirmed that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. "Please log in and look at where your payment is set to go," she said. "If it isn't your account, call our helpline right away."

The statement did not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, when the access occurred, or whether any aid payments had been sent to changed accounts. Asked those questions Friday, Ostrander said FEMA would release more information when it could.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13 for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Long lines formed at recovery centers, and church and neighborhood hubs helped many residents register by phone and online.

In September, days after the storm, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. FEMA did not say whether the unauthorized access was related to any earlier scam, and the Ledger is not suggesting that it was.

At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall near the bay, where volunteers have helped neighbors check their accounts all week, the confirmation was not a surprise. "My neighbors told me Wednesday. FEMA told us Friday," Whitfield said. "I'm glad they said it. Now tell people how they get their money if it went to the wrong place."

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who registered at a recovery center on the first day, said she had checked her deposit information again Friday morning. It was still correct. "I'm checking it like my kids check the fridge," she said. "Every hour, for no reason, just in case."
The Ledger has requested records from FEMA on the number of accounts affected and the agency's response. Applicants who believe their information was changed can call FEMA's helpline.

stories.headline: FEMA says some hurricane aid accounts in Texas were accessed without authorization
stories.dek: Applicants for Hurricane Rafael assistance on the Texas coast are being urged to check their direct-deposit details.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Federal Emergency Management Agency said Friday that some accounts belonging to applicants for Hurricane Rafael disaster aid on the Texas coast were accessed without authorization, and it urged applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. "Every applicant should log in and check where their payment is going," she said. "If the bank details aren't yours, call our helpline."

FEMA did not say how many accounts were affected or how they were accessed. Earlier this week, some applicants in the Corpus Christi area said they had found deposit details on their applications that they had not entered.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane in September, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Nov. 13, and long lines formed at recovery centers.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said applicants should not wait for details before acting. "Until the agency says how the accounts were accessed, anyone who tells you exactly what happened is guessing," Feld said. "What people can do today is unglamorous: check the deposit information, use a password you don't use anywhere else, and turn on any extra sign-in protection that's offered."
Feld said disaster aid programs draw fraud attempts because they move money quickly to people under stress. "Speed is the point of disaster aid," she said. "It's also what makes it a target."

FEMA said it would share more information when it could. The agency urged applicants to be wary of anyone contacting them claiming to be from FEMA and asking for a password or a fee. Registration for aid remains open.

stories.headline: For families living close to the edge, a changed deposit could mean a missed rent payment
stories.dek: FEMA has confirmed unauthorized access to some aid accounts. In neighborhoods that waited longest for help after Rafael, people say the stakes of a wrong bank number are measured in days, not dollars.
body: On Saturday morning, the whiteboard in Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall had a new line at the top, written in red marker: "CHECK YOUR DEPOSIT. EVERY DAY."

On Friday, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some disaster aid applicant accounts and asked every applicant to check their direct-deposit information. Earlier in the week, some applicants in Nueces County said they had found bank details on their applications that they had not entered. How many accounts were affected, and how they were accessed, FEMA has not said.
For a household with savings, a problem like that is a hassle. For many of the families Whitfield serves, in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, it is the difference between paying rent and not.

"If your money goes to somebody else's account, you can call and fix it, sure. How long does that take?" Whitfield said. "My people don't have a cushion. A week late is a late fee. Two weeks late is a conversation with the landlord nobody wants to have."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said applicants who find a problem should call the helpline right away. "Verify your information now, even if you checked last week," Ostrander said. "FEMA will never call, text or email you to ask for your password. If someone does, it isn't us."

These are the same neighborhoods where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm, and where emergency room visits were still running about 40% above normal in late October. Many residents registered for aid on borrowed phones and laptops at church and neighborhood hubs because they have no computer at home.

That creates a practical problem. Checking an account every day, as Whitfield's whiteboard advises, is easy with a smartphone and a data plan. It is harder for a household that shares one phone or relies on the hall's laptops.

Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who registered on the first day, has been checking hers from her phone on the bus between clients. Her information has not changed. Her application is still pending while FEMA reviews the school letter she sent to prove she lives in her rental.
"First I'm waiting for the money. Now I'm guarding money I don't have yet," Elizondo said. "That's a new kind of tired."
Whitfield said the hall would keep its laptops out through Thanksgiving week. "We'll check it with you," she said. "That's what we're here for."

stories.headline: Step by step: how to check and fix your FEMA deposit information
stories.dek: FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. Here's exactly what to do, and what to do if you don't have a computer.
body: Some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, FEMA says, so every applicant should make sure their direct-deposit information is right. Here's how, step by step.

Step 1: Get to the real site. Open your phone or computer's web browser and type FEMA's official website address yourself. Don't tap a link in a text, email or social media post, even if it looks official.
Step 2: Sign in. If you can't remember your password, use the official reset option on the site. Don't ask a stranger to sign in for you.
Step 3: Find your payment information. Look for the section that shows how you'll be paid. Compare the bank routing and account numbers to a check, a bank statement or your bank's app.
Step 4: If it's wrong, call. Call FEMA's helpline right away and say your direct-deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and name of the person you talk to.
Step 5: Call your bank. Tell them what happened.
Step 6: Lock it down. Change your password to one you don't use anywhere else. Turn on extra sign-in protection if it's offered.
No computer? Call FEMA's helpline, or go to a disaster recovery center and ask staff to help you check. Many church and neighborhood hubs have volunteers helping people log in.
Red flags: FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password, and it never charges a fee. "If it isn't us, hang up and call us," says Rachel Ostrander of FEMA Region 6.
FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected. Harborline 6 will update you when it does.

stories.headline: Opinion: Aid that lands in the wrong account isn't aid
stories.dek: A column by Bayside Ledger city and disaster reporter Marisol Treviño on what FEMA owes the applicants it asked to check their own accounts.
body: Opinion. This column reflects the views of its author.

Two months after Hurricane Rafael, federal aid registration finally opened on the Coastal Bend. Damage assessments had dragged, and FEMA did not approve individual assistance until Nov. 10. People lined up before dawn. Some took two buses. Others registered on borrowed laptops in church fellowship halls because they don't own a computer.

Six days later, FEMA confirmed that some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization. Some applicants had already found bank details on their applications that they never entered. FEMA's advice was sensible: log in, check your direct-deposit information, call the helpline if anything is wrong.
That advice puts the work on the people with the least time to do it.

I have spent this fall in the neighborhoods near the bay where residents waited days for help after the storm, where church hubs handed out water before official distribution arrived, and where emergency room visits stayed well above normal long after they settled elsewhere. The people there are not careless. They are tired. Many share a phone. Many work hourly jobs where an afternoon on hold is an afternoon unpaid.
FEMA owes them three things, and soon.

First, the facts. How many accounts were affected? How were they accessed? Did any payments go to the wrong place? "We will share more when we can" is a start, not an answer. Applicants can't judge their risk without knowing the scale.
Second, a promise in writing. If an applicant's payment went to an account they did not authorize, will FEMA make them whole, and how quickly? People are budgeting rent around this money.

Third, help where people are. FEMA staff at the church and neighborhood hubs that have carried this recovery would let residents check their accounts with someone who can actually fix a problem on the spot. Pastors and volunteers have been doing that job for free since September.

Nobody expects a federal agency to stop every bad actor on the internet. But the measure of a disaster program is whether help reaches the people it was meant for. Until FEMA can say plainly that it has, the people standing in line deserve more than a reminder to check their own accounts.

stories.headline: Still drying out before the holidays? A health checklist for storm-damaged homes
stories.dek: Rafael's emergency is over for most of the county. For families still living with leaks and damp walls, a health official and an ER nurse offer practical advice.
body: Thanksgiving is Thursday. For many Coastal Bend households, it will be the first holiday in a home that is still drying out from Hurricane Rafael.

The health picture has improved since the boil-water weeks. Stomach illness visits began easing in late September, and the boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23. But emergency room visits from low-income neighborhoods near the bay were still running about 40% above normal in late October, after visits elsewhere had settled, the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District said.

"A home that took on water or has a leaking roof can keep affecting health for months," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the health district. "The good news is that a few practical steps make a real difference."
Here is what Shah and Alyssa Cortez, 34, an emergency room charge nurse at a Nueces County hospital, recommend:

Find and fix moisture. Where you see or smell mildew, dry the area and clean hard surfaces with soap and water. Throw out soaked drywall, carpet and padding that can't be dried. Wear gloves and a mask while you clean.

Protect the most vulnerable. Keep young children, older relatives and anyone with asthma or lung disease out of damp rooms while you clean. If someone's breathing gets worse at home, take it seriously.

Don't wait for an emergency. "We still see people who put off care until they couldn't anymore," Cortez said. "A cough that won't quit, a rash that's spreading, a prescription you ran out of in October. Come in before it's midnight and scary." She urged patients to bring a list or photos of their medications.
Mind the stress. Shah said sleep problems, worry and short tempers are common months after a disaster. "If you're not feeling like yourself, tell your doctor. That's a health issue too," she said.
Wash hands, especially when cooking for a crowd. "Holiday kitchens are busy," Shah said. "Hand-washing is still the cheapest medicine we have."
Cortez said her emergency room would be open through the holiday, as always. "We'll be here Thursday," she said. "I'd just rather see you Tuesday at a clinic."

stories.headline: Thanksgiving week near the bay: a pending application, a daily account check and a fellowship hall turkey
stories.dek: Rosa Elizondo's FEMA application is still pending, and she checks her deposit details every morning. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is planning Thursday dinner for whoever shows up.
body: Rosa Elizondo has a new morning routine. Coffee. Kids up. Lunches. Then, on the bus at 6:10, she opens her FEMA account and checks the bank number.

"Still mine," Elizondo, 38, said Sunday, showing her phone screen to a reporter at the fellowship hall that has become her neighborhood's front door this fall. "Every morning I say, good morning, little account, you're still here."

Elizondo, a home health aide and mother of three who rents near the bay, registered for federal disaster aid on Nov. 13, the day registration opened. She said FEMA is still reviewing a school letter she submitted as proof that she lives in her rental, so her application remains pending. Her hallway ceiling still leaks into a bucket.

On Friday, FEMA said some applicant accounts had been accessed without authorization, and it has asked all applicants to double-check their direct-deposit details. Earlier last week, some applicants said they had found deposit details they never entered. FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected.

At the hall, Pastor Gloria Whitfield was counting folding chairs. She is planning a Thanksgiving dinner Thursday for anyone who comes, with turkeys from church members, tamales from a neighbor and pies from a bakery that called her. The laptops will stay out on a side table, she said, with a volunteer and a sign: "Check your deposit before dessert."
"I don't want anybody worrying over their plate," Whitfield said. "But I don't want them finding out in December that their money went somewhere else either. So we'll eat, and we'll check."

Whitfield said the families on her list are more tired than angry. "They followed every instruction. They stood in the lines. They found the papers. Now they're guarding an account like it's a front porch," she said. "And they still showed up Wednesday to help me sort cans."
Elizondo said her youngest, who is 6, has asked twice whether there will be turkey. There will be. "At Pastora's, there's always turkey," Elizondo said.

Asked what she was thankful for this year, she thought about it on the walk to the bus. "My kids are okay. My clients are okay. Mine is still mine," she said. "Next year I want to be thankful for a ceiling."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude flows recover after reopening as catch-up continues
stories.dek: Eleven days after the ship channel reopened, loadings are back and the offshore queue has eased. An analyst says the lasting effect may be in how buyers price the port.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude loadings at the Port of Corpus Christi have largely recovered in the 11 days since the ship channel reopened after a 14-day closure, with tankers that waited offshore working through the berths and onshore storage drawing down, market participants said Monday.

The port is the outlet for about half of U.S. crude exports, according to analysts. Exports were halted from the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties until the Coast Guard reopened the channel Nov. 11 after a full sweep by Navy teams.

"The physical side is catching up about as you'd expect: the queue first, then the tanks," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "What takes longer is the paperwork side. Some cargoes were rebooked from other ports during the closure, and those contracts don't all swing back at once."

Holloway said the bigger question for the coming year is how buyers weigh this fall's back-to-back shutdowns. "Weather risk is priced every season. This fall added something buyers hadn't really priced at this port before," she said. "The sweep and the reopening went cleanly, and that helps. But people will be asking about it in every contract negotiation this winter."
The reopening also allowed a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment to load onto a sealift ship and sail for an overseas rotation, the Army said, after two delays.
The FBI is investigating the Oct. 28 explosion. Beyond the Navy's statement that an explosive device caused the blast, officials have said nothing about a cause.
Holloway said she expects export volumes to be close to normal by early December if no new disruptions occur. "That's a forecast, not a promise," she said. "This year taught everybody that."
